turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Love that you’re getting into roses! Let me break the main choices down very simply.

Choose roses that fit your climate
Every rose is labeled with hardiness zones.
At the top of our site you can pick your zone (for example, Zone 5 or Zone 8). That will show you roses that can handle your winters.
Decide how much sun your spot gets
Full sun: 6 or more hours of direct sun. Most roses prefer this.
Partial shade: about 4 hours of sun. Look for roses marked as being okay with partial shade.
Pick the style of rose you want A few big categories:
Climbing roses: Grow tall and need support (arches, fences, walls). Great if you want a vertical feature.
Shrub/bush roses: Rounded, bushy plants that fill a space or border. Good for most gardens.
Groundcover/landscape roses: Low, spreading plants that cover the ground and make a simple, flower-filled area.
Hybrid tea roses: Classic “long-stemmed” type with one big bloom per stem, great for cutting and vases.
Think about how you’ll use them
For cutting and bringing indoors: Hybrid teas and some floribundas (lots of blooms) are great.
For a big show in the garden: Shrub roses, floribundas, and climbers.
For fragrance: Use the fragrance filter on the site to pick strongly scented varieties.
How our roses arrive
All of our roses are own-root (no graft or bud union) and come in 1-gallon containers with soil.
They are shipped without leaves or buds, which is normal; they leaf out once planted and settled in.

What do beginners usually say about it in reviews?

Newer gardeners tend to say a lot of the same things in their reviews, so there are some clear patterns.

Here’s what beginners usually mention:

How the rose arrives
They’re often surprised it comes without leaves or buds, then relieved when it starts to leaf out and grow.
Many say the plant looked small at first but took off once planted in the right spot.
Ease of care
Beginners frequently mention being nervous at first, then happy that the rose “just kept growing” with basic watering and sun.
People appreciate that our roses are own-root (no graft) because they handle setbacks better and grow back from their own roots.
Blooming
A common theme is how exciting that first flush of blooms is.
New growers often say they got more flowers than expected in the first year, especially with repeat or continuous bloomers.
Learning curve
Many beginners say they were intimidated, but that planting and basic care were much simpler than they thought once they followed the instructions.
Some mention that small mistakes (like a missed watering or less-than-perfect pruning) didn’t ruin the plant, which makes them feel more confident.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question. I’ll keep this really simple so your very first time goes smoothly.

I’m going to assume “it” is your first rose. If you meant a specific product (like the Get Growing Bundle or Founders Fish Fertilizer), tell me which one and I’ll explain that too.

Here’s how to use your new rose properly the first time:

Decide where it will live
Pick a spot with:
At least 6 hours of sun if possible (full sun), or
At least 4 hours if the rose is labeled as okay in partial shade.
Make sure water does not pool there after rain.
Check your planting timing
Roses should go in the ground:
After your last spring frost, or
At least 6 weeks before your first fall frost.
If you tell me your ZIP code, I can tell you whether you should plant in the ground now or temporarily grow it in a larger pot first.
Prepare the planting hole (for ground planting)
Dig a hole about 2 feet wide and 2 feet deep.
Mix the top soil you removed with some organic matter (like compost) to improve structure.
Put some of that mix back into the hole so the rose will sit at the same level it was in the pot.
Take the rose out of its pot
Our roses are own-root and come in 1-gallon containers with soil.
Gently squeeze the sides of the pot and slide the rose out while supporting the base.
Loosen the roots slightly with your fingers if they are tightly circling.
Plant it at the right height
Set the rose into the hole so the top of the root ball is level with the surrounding soil.
Backfill around it with your amended soil, pressing gently to remove air pockets.
Water deeply
Water slowly at the base until the soil is thoroughly soaked.
For the first few weeks, keep the soil consistently moist but not soggy:
Usually watering 2–3 times per week, depending on heat and rainfall.
Mulch around the base
Add a 2–3 inch layer of mulch (like compost or fine bark) on top of the soil, keeping it about 3 inches away from the base of the rose.
This helps keep roots cool and moist.
Keep it outdoors only
Very important: roses must be grown outdoors. Do not keep them indoors, even “just for a while,” because they need natural conditions and winter dormancy.
